topic: The Logic of Light: A Calculus-Based Proof of Snell's Law
target_audience: University students or advanced high school students with a basic understanding of calculus and optics.

outline.topic: The Logic of Light: A Calculus-Based Proof of Snell's Law
outline.target_audience: University students or advanced high school students with a basic understanding of calculus and optics.

sections.title: The Refraction Mystery
sections.content: Introduce the phenomenon of refraction where light bends at the interface of two media. Define the goal: to prove why light follows a specific path using Fermat's Principle of Least Time. Visually present the transition of a light ray from Air (Medium 1) to Water (Medium 2).
sections.example: A visual of a 'Laser Cat' pointing a laser into a fish tank, showing the beam visibly 'breaking' or bending as it hits the water surface.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Fermat’s Principle
sections.content: Establish the foundational rule: Light always takes the path that requires the least amount of time. Explain that because the speed of light (v) varies in different media (v = c/n), the straight-line distance is not always the fastest route.
sections.example: A split-screen animation showing a 'Lifeguard' running on sand (fast) and swimming in water (slow). To reach a drowning swimmer, the lifeguard doesn't run in a straight line; they run further on sand to minimize the time spent in the water.

sections.title: Setting Up the Geometric Model
sections.content: Create a coordinate system. Point A is at (0, a) in Medium 1. Point B is at (w, -b) in Medium 2. The light hits the interface at point (x, 0). Express the distances d1 (hypotenuse in Medium 1) and d2 (hypotenuse in Medium 2) using the Pythagorean theorem in terms of x.
sections.example: A clear geometric diagram showing two triangles. d1 = sqrt(x² + a²) and d2 = sqrt((w-x)² + b²), with angles θ1 and θ2 labeled relative to the normal line.

sections.title: The Time Function
sections.content: Formulate the total travel time T(x) as the sum of time spent in both media: T = (d1/v1) + (d2/v2). Substitute the distance expressions into the equation to create a single-variable function T(x).
sections.example: An overlay of the mathematical formula: T(x) = [sqrt(x² + a²) / v1] + [sqrt((w-x)² + b²) / v2]. Highlight the variable 'x' as the point that light 'chooses' to minimize time.

sections.title: Optimization via Calculus
sections.content: To find the minimum time, take the derivative of T with respect to x and set it to zero (dT/dx = 0). Show the step-by-step differentiation of the square root terms, resulting in x / (v1 * d1) - (w-x) / (v2 * d2) = 0.
sections.example: An animated sliding point 'x' on the boundary. As 'x' moves, a graph of T(x) above it shifts, showing the 'dip' where the derivative is zero.

sections.title: Connecting Geometry to Trigonometry
sections.content: Identify that x/d1 is exactly sin(θ1) and (w-x)/d2 is exactly sin(θ2) based on the triangles from Section 3. Substitute these into the derivative equation to get sin(θ1)/v1 = sin(θ2)/v2.
sections.example: The geometric diagram from earlier pulses the 'opposite' side and 'hypotenuse' of the triangles to visually link the ratio to the sine function.

sections.title: The Final Arrival: Snell’s Law
sections.content: Replace the velocities (v) with the refractive index formula (v = c/n). Show how (sin(θ1) / (c/n1)) = (sin(θ2) / (c/n2)) simplifies to the final form: n1 * sin(θ1) = n2 * sin(θ2).
sections.example: A 'Formula Forge' animation where the variables clink together and simplify into the golden equation: n1 sinθ1 = n2 sinθ2, surrounded by a glowing aura of success.

storyboard.title: The Refraction Mystery
lecture_lines: Ever noticed light bending as it enters water?
This phenomenon is known as refraction.
Why does light choose this specific path?
animations: Create a horizontal interface line at y=0. Label 'Air' (#FFFFFF) above and 'Water' (#00BFFF) below.
Animate a yellow light ray (#FFFF00) from point A(0, 2) to the interface at (x,0).
Animate the ray bending towards the normal line (#A9A9A9) as it enters the water towards Point B.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: Fermat’s Principle
lecture_lines: Light follows the path of least time.
Speed changes when light enters a new medium.
The fastest path isn't always a straight line.
animations: Display a split screen: sand (#F4A460) on top, water (#1E90FF) on bottom.
Show a 'lifeguard' icon moving along a path that bends at the interface to minimize total travel time.
Display the text 'Fermat\\'s Principle: Least Time' in the center (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Setting Up the Geometric Model
lecture_lines: Place point A in air and B in water.
Light hits the interface at some point x.
Use Pythagoras to find distance in air.
Repeat this for the distance in water.
Distances are now expressed in terms of x.
animations: Draw a 2D coordinate system. Label Point A at (0, a) and Point B at (w, -b).
Place a point X at (x, 0) on the horizontal interface line.
Draw yellow segments (#FFFF00) d1 (A to X) and d2 (X to B). Label them.
Label the horizontal segments on the x-axis as 'x' and 'w-x' in white (#FFFFFF).
Show the distance formulas d1 = sqrt(x^2 + a^2) and d2 = sqrt((w-x)^2 + b^2) using LaTeX (#FFFF00).

storyboard.title: The Time Function
lecture_lines: Total time is distance divided by velocity.
Sum the travel times for both media.
We have a time function depending on x.
animations: Display the total time equation T(x) = T1 + T2 in the top center (#FFFFFF).
Expand the equation to T(x) = d1/v1 + d2/v2, using colors for v1 (#00FF00) and v2 (#00FFFF).
Substitute the square root expressions for d1 and d2 into the T(x) formula.

storyboard.title: Optimization via Calculus
lecture_lines: To minimize time, set the derivative to zero.
Differentiate the time function with respect to x.
Use the chain rule for the square roots.
Set the simplified expression equal to zero.
This equation defines the fastest possible path.
animations: Show the derivative notation dT/dx = 0 in bold yellow (#FFFF00) to signify optimization.
Step-by-step differentiation: Show d/dx of the first term resulting in x / (v1 * d1).
Show d/dx of the second term resulting in -(w-x) / (v2 * d2) using the chain rule.
Combine the terms to form the equation: x / (v1 * d1) - (w-x) / (v2 * d2) = 0.
Animate point x sliding on the x-axis, while a T(x) graph above shows a minimum at that point.

storyboard.title: Connecting Geometry to Trigonometry
lecture_lines: Look back at our geometric triangles.
These ratios are sines of the angles.
Substitute sines into our calculus result.
animations: Highlight the right-angled triangles in the geometry: pulse the opposite side 'x' and hypotenuse 'd1'.
Display the trigonometric relations sin(theta1) = x/d1 and sin(theta2) = (w-x)/d2 (#FFFFFF).
Substitute these ratios into the derivative equation: sin(theta1)/v1 = sin(theta2)/v2 (#FFD700).

storyboard.title: The Final Arrival: Snell’s Law
lecture_lines: Light speed in a medium depends on index n.
Replace velocity with the refractive index formula.
The constant speed of light cancels from both sides.
Rearrange the terms into their final form.
We have derived Snell's Law from first principles.
animations: Recall the refractive index definition: v = c / n. Display this formula (#FFFFFF).
Substitute v1 = c/n1 and v2 = c/n2 into the simplified derivative equation.
Show the algebra: sin(theta1) / (c/n1) = sin(theta2) / (c/n2).
Cancel the speed of light 'c' from both sides of the equation.
Display the final form: n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2) with a glowing highlight effect (#FFD700).
